deep.reconstruction:
Context. This is the cover leaf of an 8-leaf gathering (archival note '[8 Bl.] 3-10'). It holds pencil working notes from practical astronomy with a meridian transit instrument (Passageninstrument), apparently at Göttingen. The next page discusses the middle thread, thread intervals, collimation error and screw value. Nothing on the page concerns air waves (Luftwellen) or any mathematical theory. These are observing and reduction scraps.

(1) Setting formula. '88° 34′' is a rough declination of Polaris (α UMi) for the 1850s. The heading '90° + φ − δ' is the reading at which the altitude/setting circle must be set to find a star of declination δ in the meridian. Here φ is the latitude of Göttingen, φ ≈ 51°31′48″, so 90° + φ = 141°31′48″.

(2) Polaris. The subtraction on the page is 141°3x′48″ − 88°3x′6″ = 52°59′42″, i.e. reading = 90° + φ − δ(Polaris).
- With the Göttingen value 141°31′48″, the written result 52°59′42″ requires δ = 88°32′6″. That is a correct apparent declination of Polaris around 1854–56.
- So the digits read as 38′/39′ are very probably 31′/32′. The arithmetic also works with the literal reading 141°38′48″ − 88°39′6″, since both minutes shift equally.
- The result is rounded to 52°59′.
- The '57′7' written below is unclear. It may be an alternative setting allowing for a collimation/index correction (compare '+ Coll. fehl.' on the next page). I cannot reconstruct it with certainty.

(3) ν Piscium. 'ν Piscium 136°45′36″, 136°47′' is the same setting computed for ν Psc.
- The marginal '4° 46′ …' is its declination. 141°31′48″ − 4°46′12″ = 136°45′36″, so the marginal figure is probably 4°46′12″ (the '.422' is a misreading).
- ν Psc has J2000 δ ≈ +5°29′. Precessing back about 145 years at roughly 18″/yr gives δ ≈ +4°46′ in the mid-1850s, which is consistent.
- 136°47′ is a rounded or corrected setting.

(4) Polaris transit. 'α Urs. min. O.C. 23. Nov.' records an upper culmination (obere Culmination) of Polaris on 23 November, by clock times of passage over the threads 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. Thread 4, the middle thread, was missed.
- Successive intervals: 6m58s, 6m46s, then 13m41s (two intervals), 7m10s, 6m43s.
- These huge intervals come from the factor sec δ ≈ 1/cos(88°32′) ≈ 39 multiplying equatorial thread intervals of about 10–11 s. The next page uses factors ≈ 39.5, consistent with this.
- Mean of the six times (my computation): 4115 s = 1h 8m 35s clock time. This works for a symmetric thread system.
- 'Jedenfalls 1h 3' may be a rough expected right ascension (Polaris α ≈ 1h3m–1h5m in the 1850s) or a clock-correction estimate. Unsure.
errors: No arithmetic error: 141°3x′48″ − 88°3x′06″ = 52°59′42″ is correct whichever equal minute digits are read.

With Göttingen φ = 51°31′48″ the minute digits must be 31′ and 32′. If the image genuinely reads 38′/39′, the latitude used would be wrong (51°38′). This is most likely a transcription issue, not Riemann's.

Thread 4 (middle thread) missing; the reduction must rely on thread symmetry or known thread intervals. The scatter of the intervals (6m43s to 7m10s) reflects timing error, amplified by the sec δ factor of about 39.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine observing and reduction notes from practical astronomy at a transit instrument (Göttingen latitude, Polaris and ν Psc). No mathematical content beyond sexagesimal subtraction. It is mildly interesting biographically that Riemann did such exercises, but there is nothing novel.

checkable.asserts: 90°+φ−δ for Polaris with φ=51°31′48″ and δ=88°32′6″ gives 52°59′42″
The literal transcription's subtraction also gives 52°59′42″
Setting for ν Piscium with δ=4°46′12″ is 136°45′36″
Mean of the six thread times = 4115 s = 1h8m35s
sec δ for Polaris ≈ 39.1, explaining ~7 min thread intervals from ~10.5 s equatorial intervals

transcription_corrections: '88° 39′ 6″' is most likely 88° 32′ 6″ (apparent δ of Polaris, mid-1850s).
'4° 46,422″' is probably 4° 46′ 12″ (declination of ν Piscium), consistent with 136°45′36″.
'O.C.' = obere Culmination (upper culmination); 'Fad' = Faden (thread of the transit instrument); 'v. Piscium' = ν Piscium.
